name: Unity Principle
description: People are more readily influenced by others they perceive as sharing their identity or group membership ('we-ness') -- a distinct mechanism from ordinary liking, explained by shared identity making a source's norms and requests feel self-relevant rather than merely likeable.
design_relevance_note: Cialdini's seventh, most recently added persuasion principle -- relevant to community-framed products, cohort/team-based onboarding, 'people like you' social proof framing, identity-based marketing segmentation, and co-creation features that position the user as part of a shared in-group with the brand or other users.
prevalence_note: Named explicitly in persuasion/marketing discourse following Cialdini's own popularization as his newest principle, but considerably less established in mainstream design-practice vocabulary than his other six principles (Reciprocity, Commitment & Consistency, Social Proof, Authority, Scarcity, Liking).

findings.description: Reviewing classic and recent social-influence research through self-categorization theory, Spears argues that a shared group identity changes influence because group norms become self-relevant: when people see a source as part of 'us,' persuasion/conformity is explained less by interpersonal liking alone and more by identification with the group and its norms. The strength of this identity-based influence depends on moderators such as degree of group identification, intragroup/intergroup context, and whether interaction is anonymous, visible, isolated, or co-present.

applications.title: A teacher and a principal use the IKEA effect deliberately to build school culture
applications.description: Writing together, a classroom teacher (Cathleen Beachboard) and a school principal (Nick Brousse) describe using the IKEA effect deliberately as a school-culture strategy: having students co-create their own classroom community principles and behavior norms (rather than being handed a rulebook), involving teacher leaders in vetting new hires so new colleagues are seen as 'our teammate' rather than 'the administration's hire,' and using student advisory groups to shape event planning and school-climate initiatives. They frame the underlying mechanism explicitly around IKEA-effect research (including findings that even young children value self-built objects more, independent of ownership or effort alone) and contrast compliance-based systems (imposed, complied with) against ownership-based ones (co-created, protected).
applications.industry_context: K-12 education, school leadership and culture
applications.ethical_note: Deliberately invoking the IKEA effect here builds genuine shared ownership and belonging among students and staff, not a manipulation of an end user for a third party's commercial benefit.

applications.title: Cialdini's own restaurant example: asking for 'advice' beat asking for 'opinions'
applications.description: In his book Pre-Suasion, Robert Cialdini describes an experiment involving a restaurant concept called 'Splash!': after being shown a description of the concept, consumers were asked for either their 'advice,' 'opinions,' or 'expectations' regarding it, then asked how likely they'd be to visit. Those asked for 'advice' reported significantly higher intent to visit than those asked for opinions or expectations -- Cialdini's explanation, quoted directly in this CXL article, is that giving advice puts a person in a 'merging state of mind' that links their own identity with the company's (unity/co-creation), while giving an opinion keeps them in a separate, self-focused frame.
applications.ethical_note: Framing a feedback request as seeking 'advice' to build a sense of co-created ownership is a subtle persuasion technique -- genuinely useful for building real customer relationships, but also usable to manufacture a feeling of unity that isn't matched by the company actually acting on the input.
